skardu.story: Traveller, as you come to Skardu, you find a city in Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan in the disputed Kashmir region, serving as the capital of Skardu District and the Baltistan Division. It sits at nearly 2,500 metres above sea level in the Skardu Valley, at the confluence of the Indus and Shigar rivers, and is an important gateway to the eight-thousanders of the nearby Karakoram, while the Indus River running through the region separates the Karakoram from the Ladakh Range. Its name is believed to come from the Balti word meaning “a lowland between two high places,” referring to Shigar city and Satpara Lake. The valley is 10 kilometres wide and 40 kilometres long, linked to the main Karakoram Highway via the Baltistan Highway.
skardu.name: Skardu

skardu-fort.story: Skardu Fort, or Kharpocho—the king of forts—stands in Skardu in the Gilgit-Baltistan region of Pakistan, above the junction of the Indus and Shigar rivers and overlooking the Rock of Skardu. Its earliest structure was built by king Ali Sher Khan Anchan at the end of the 16th century, and the Mendoq Khar palace of his Ladakhi queen, Mandok Gyalmo, is located just beside the fort. It mainly served as a military stronghold and strategic lookout and remained the centre of the Maqpon dynasty until the fall of Maqpon monarch Ahmad Shah at the hands of the Dogras in the 19th century. During his invasion of Baltistan in 1840, Dogra general Zorawar Singh stormed and razed it and built another fort on level ground next to the Kharpocho hill; later, in the first Indo-Pakistan War of 1947–1948, it was besieged by the Ibex Force and Chitral Scouts under Col. Mata ul-Mulk, and the Jammu and Kashmir State Forces under Lt. Col. Sher Jung Thapa eventually surrendered after running out of rations on 14 August 1948, a year after independence of Pakistan.
skardu-fort.name: Skardu Fort

satpara-lake.story: Traveller, as you come to Satpara Lake near Skardu in Gilgit-Baltistan, you’ll find a natural lake at 2,600 m above sea level, spanning 4 km² with a picturesque island. It is fed by melting glacial ice from the surrounding mountains and by melting snow from the Deosai Plains, while its only outlet, the Satpara Stream, supplies water to Skardu Valley and drains into the Indus River. Traditional accounts attribute the damming of the lake to the Balti king Ali Senge Anchan, while his queen Mandok Gyalmo took the stream out of it to irrigate her gardens. The completion of Satpara Dam downstream has enlarged the lake, and it provides habitat to the brown and rainbow trout fishes introduced in the region.
satpara-lake.name: Satpara Lake

manthal-buddha-rock.story: In Manthal village in Skardu, Pakistan, you can find Manthal Buddha Rock, called “Dray chatfi Fong” in Balti, a large granite rock with a relief sculpture of Buddha that probably dates back to the 8th century. It is one of the most important relics of Skardu and is about 3 km from the Sadpara Road that leads to Satpara Lake. Before the arrival of Islam in Gilgit-Baltistan, the majority of the people were Buddhist and sculpted Buddha images on many rocks, but this carving was not known to the world until the beginning of the 20th century due to its remote location. In 1906 the Scottish traveller Alice Christie wrote a book and featured the carving, giving it international attention; since then the government has taken steps to preserve it, it is visited by tourists who visit Skardu, and recently the Pakistani government has been attempting to promote religious travel and recognise these sacred sites in national forums to inform the global Buddhist community.
manthal-buddha-rock.name: Manthal Buddha Rock

katpana-desert.story: Traveller, let the Katpana Desert welcome you—also known as Biang-a Naqpo, Katpana Biang-a, or the Skardu Cold Desert—a high-altitude desert in Skardu Valley in Skardu District, Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan. At 2,226 m above sea level, it is one of the highest deserts in the world, where large sand dunes are covered in snow during the winter. The most frequented portion lies near Katpana Lake close to Skardu International Airport, while the desert stretches from the banks of the Indus River in the south of Skardu to New Ranga Village in the north. Here temperatures reach a maximum of 27 °C and a minimum in October of 8 °C, dropping below −17 °C in December and January and occasionally as low as −25 °C.
katpana-desert.name: Katpana Desert

lower-kachura-lake.story: Traveller, when you reach Lower Kachura Lake, also known as Shangrila Lake, near Skardu in Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan, you are at 2,500 metres. On its bank, an operational resort has welcomed tourists since 1983, and the Shangrila Resort Hotel was established that year as the first resort hotel in Skardu. Founded by Aslam Khan Afridi, a Pakistani military officer who served as the first commander of the Northern Scouts, it is now chaired by his son, Arif Aslam Khan, and is known for a restaurant built in the fuselage of an aircraft that crashed nearby. With the resort’s architecture and the background Karakoram hills, the lake’s landscapes make it one of northern Pakistan’s attractive tourist destinations, and its name comes from Shangri-La, the idyllic Himalayan paradise in James Hilton’s 1933 novel Lost Horizon, a Tibetan-language word meaning “heaven on Earth.”
lower-kachura-lake.name: Lower Kachura Lake

kachura-lake.story: Traveller, in the Skardu District of Gilgit-Baltistan, northern Pakistan, three lakes sit at 2,500 metres in the Karakoram mountain range of the western Himalayas, in the greater Baltistan Region and the Indus River basin. Foroq Tso, or Upper Kachura Lake, has clear water and a depth of 70 metres; in summer it has a temperature of 15 °C, and in winter the surface is frozen solid. Its beauty is almost untampered and mostly unexplored by travellers due to lack of infrastructure owing to its rough terrain, but the area has a rich flora of the Western Himalayan subalpine conifer forests ecoregion and wild apricot—Prunus armeniaca—orchards. Recreation at Foroq Tso or Upper Kachura Lake includes hiking, trout fishing, and Himalaya mountaineering, with the upper Indus River flowing nearby at a lower elevation.
kachura-lake.name: Upper Kachura Lake

shigar-palace.story: In the town of Shigar, Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan, the Shigar Palace, also known as Fong Khar, or “The Palace on the Rock,” is an old palace about 30 kilometres from Skardu on the way to Baltoro Glacier and K2, the second highest mountain on Earth. The current structure was originally built in the 17th century by the 20th Raja of the Amacha Dynasty of Shigar on a large boulderstone, and it was called Fong Khar, meaning “Palace on the Rock.” It has been restored by Aga Khan Cultural Service Pakistan, the Pakistan arm of the Aga Khan Historic Cities Programme, and after restoration it was converted to a heritage museum and luxury hotel managed by Serena Hotels. The restoration took place from 1999 to 2004 and cost approximately US$1.4 million, and in 2006 the fort won the UNESCO Asia Pacific Heritage Award for its cultural heritage conservation.
shigar-palace.name: Shigar Palace
